lesson.title: Speed vs. Velocity: What the Sign Tells You
lesson.summary: Velocity is signed, positive or negative depending on direction, while speed is its absolute value and is always zero or positive; the same speed can correspond to two opposite velocities.
lesson.body:
In everyday conversation, speed and velocity often get used as if they mean the same thing. In calculus they don't. Velocity is a signed number: positive or negative, depending on which way along the line of motion the object is heading. Speed only reports magnitude, how fast, with the direction information deliberately thrown away.

Speed at time t is defined as speed(t) = |v(t)|, the absolute value of velocity. Because absolute value output is never negative, speed can never be negative either; if a computation ever produces a negative speed, that's a sign an error was made somewhere upstream.

Using v(t) = 3t^2 - 12t + 9 from the running example, s(t) = t^3 - 6t^2 + 9t, recall that v(0) = 9 m/s and v(2) = -3 m/s. Speed at these same instants is speed(0) = |9| = 9 m/s and speed(2) = |-3| = 3 m/s. So at t = 0 the object's velocity and speed happen to match, both 9, since the velocity was already positive there, but at t = 2 they diverge: velocity is -3 while speed is 3.

The clearest way to see why the distinction matters is this: a velocity of +9 m/s and a velocity of -9 m/s describe motion at the exact same speed, 9 m/s, but in opposite directions. Speed alone can never tell these two situations apart; you would need the signed velocity to know which way the object is actually headed. That signed information, and how to read it, is exactly the subject of the next chapter.
